subject: science
passage: Moon jellyfish spend part of their lives as polyps, tiny stalks attached to rocks or piers. In winter, each polyp divides into a stack of discs that break away one by one as young jellyfish, a process called strobilation. Marine biologist Ingrid Solberg has found that in one Norwegian fjord, the release of young jellyfish starts on different dates from year to year. She hypothesizes that the timing depends mainly on when the water cools below a particular temperature, not on how much plankton, the polyps' food, is available at the time.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Solberg's hypothesis?

choices.A: In laboratory tanks cooled in the same way, polyps given very different amounts of food began strobilation at about the same time.
choices.B: Young jellyfish released in the fjord grow faster in years when plankton is plentiful than in years when it is scarce.
choices.C: Polyps in the fjord are found mostly on the shaded undersides of floating piers rather than on open rocks.
choices.D: In years with abundant plankton, release began earlier in the fjord even when the water cooled at the usual time.

explanation.why: Solberg claims that temperature, not food supply, sets when strobilation begins. Support must hold temperature constant while food varies and show that the timing does not change. In the tank test, polyps cooled the same way began at the same time despite very different food amounts.
explanation.A: Correct. Large differences in food did not change the timing when cooling was the same, which points to temperature as the controlling factor.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This concerns how fast the young jellyfish grow after release, not what sets the date of release.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Where polyps attach says nothing about whether temperature or food controls the timing of strobilation.
explanation.D: Incorrect. If plentiful food moved the release earlier with temperature unchanged, food would matter, which weakens the hypothesis.
